METHOD: Boil the milk the night before and let it cool to room temperature. In a kneading trough or a large basin, place our sifted flour and the semolina. Make a small well and add the salt. Then, gradually add the milk and mix with your hands until you have a mixture. Add flour if needed. We don't want to form a dough. Rub the mixture with your hands and let it rest for a little while (about half an hour). Place a clean tablecloth on a table, and there we will pass the trahanas through the special sieve. Transfer a small amount to the sieve and rub with your hands in circular motions on the surface of the sieve until the entire quantity has passed through to the bottom. If some pieces do not pass through, transfer them back to the trough and rub them again, adding a little flour. When we have passed all the mixture through, transfer the trahanas onto a clean sheet or tablecloth and spread it out on a bed or a large table in a shady place away from flies or other bugs. If this is not possible, cover it with tulle. Spread it in a thin layer so that it can dry. We leave it for about three or four days, stirring it occasionally. When it has dried, we pass it through the sifting screen to remove the excess flour and place it in a cloth bag or a glass jar.

eng_translated0: Kokoretsi is made with sykotaries and anteries. The sykotaria consists of the liver, the sweetbreads, the heart, and the two lungs (plemonia). These are its edible parts; however, a whole sykotaria also includes the esophagus, the diaphragm, and fat, which, although not eaten, we must definitely see attached to the other ingredients when we buy a sykotaria, and we ask the butcher to remove them. The anteria are the intestines that will wrap the kokoretsi and we buy them by the kilo. For a kokoretsi for 6-8 people, we will need 4 sykotaries, 5-6 kilos of anteries, 2-3 sweetbreads, and 2 bolies, all from a milk-fed lamb. The preparation of the anteria and the sykotaria is as follows: We carefully plug the end of each intestine and place it under running tap water. The rest of the intestine is coiled in the sink. Once some water has passed through, we remove the intestine from the tap and press it with our fingers so that the water inside travels along its entire length and removes any impurities. We repeat this process 4-5 times for each intestine, until the water comes out completely clear. Then, we put the washed intestines in a large bowl and pour plenty of lemon juice over them. We cut all the parts of the sykotaria into pieces that are as square as possible, and the sweetbreads into smaller and more numerous pieces, because we will place them frequently between the other pieces. We begin to thread the pieces of the sykotaria onto the spit, one by one, starting with a piece of sweetbread. We place them alternately and, every two or three pieces, we thread a piece of sweetbread, so that its fat is evenly distributed throughout the kokoretsi. Then we wrap the kokoretsi with the anteries. Next, we pull one bolia by its end that sticks out of the bowl and tie it to one end of the kokoretsi with a regular knot, but carefully, so it doesn't tear. Slowly turning the spit's crank with one hand, we carefully stretch the tied bolia along the length of the kokoretsi, reaching its other end. We wrap the end carefully and continue wrapping lengthwise. We continue the lengthwise wrapping until we have covered almost all the large bulges of the kokoretsi with the intestine. After 1-2 large bolies that we wrapped lengthwise, we begin to wrap the kokoretsi crosswise, at denser intervals. After the crosswise wrapping, we begin the final wrapping, with completely parallel and dense wraps.

eng_translated0: We will make Farsala Halva with butter, an easy and delicious treat! We will need 4 cups sugar (very fine granulated), 4 cups water, 2 cups cornstarch or corn flour (level), 3/4 cup sunflower oil or melted and cold milk butter (for non-fasting periods), 1 cup almond kernels (whole blanched almonds), Vanilla or cinnamon optionally for aroma. First, we toast the almonds spread out on a baking tray without their skins. Bake on the fan setting in a preheated oven at 200°C, on the middle rack for about 10 minutes until they are lightly golden. Stir during baking so they cook evenly. Set them aside. Before we begin, we keep 1 cup of sugar for the caramel and half a cup of sugar for the finishing. In a bowl, pour the remaining sugar (2.5 cups), the cornstarch, and stir. Add the water and the sunflower oil (or the melted clarified butter) and mix the ingredients very well at the beginning with a spoon so that the ingredients dissolve well and combine. Then with a whisk, stir for 2-3 minutes until the mixture of wet ingredients is smooth. If you are adding cinnamon or vanilla, you will add it at this stage. In a deep pot, pour the 1 cup of sugar gradually and over medium heat. Let it melt, stirring when necessary, with an oiled wooden spoon. When the sugar has melted evenly, then carefully add the mixture. The moment we pour in the mixture, because the temperature drops, it freezes and solidifies. However, with continuous stirring on the heat, it will return to a liquid state. Stir again and again in the pot, always on medium heat until all the liquids are absorbed and it pulls away from the sides of the pot. Remove from the heat and continue stirring for a few minutes, until the oil that rises to its surface completely disappears. Finally, once it is homogenized and smooth, then we add the toasted almonds and gently stir to distribute them everywhere. We will use a shallow baking pan, about 32 or 34 cm. The mixture should not be deep, so that its surface can caramelize nicely. We pour it into the pan. Shake the pan so that its surface spreads out and evens. Let it puff up. Sprinkle the entire surface with the remaining fine sugar (1/2 cup). Burn the sugar with a kitchen torch to caramelize it.
